about: The page for the Vireo case. Its domain, company, title, question and outcome live in hub/site.config.mjs (CASES). Every number, name and quote below is in the output files under skills/*/examples/vireo. The ending is read from the readout itself at build time. The flagged-prototype step is empty until that example exists: give it findings and a changed line then.
intro: Vireo makes AI meeting recaps. After every meeting its Recap feature writes a summary, the decisions and the action items, and hosts do not trust it enough to send it on. This is one piece of work on that problem, followed from the first question to the test result, with every document open to read.

company.customer: Priya Raman, the host of a 42 minute pricing review with Northgate

steps.question: How do other recap products get from the recap arriving to sending it on?

findings.text: Four products, three stages, 24 screens and 66 notes. Vireo had the lowest mean score of the four, 2.0. Parley had the highest, 4.13.
Vireo sends first and asks later. Its email says "Sent to all 9 invitees at 10:47". Its Share dialog then asks "Choose who gets this recap", with all 9 already selected.
Nothing on Vireo's page lets a reader check a line. The only evidence is a 42 minute recording, and one Decisions list holds what was settled beside what was only raised.

moment.label: Two of Vireo's own screens disagree
moment.note: The dialog asks who gets the recap after it has gone. The teardown found it by comparing a screen in the first stage with one in the third.

steps.changed: It marked four gaps P0. Two of them became the first release in the PRD: hold the recap for the host, and split what was decided from what was only raised.

steps.question: Why do hosts not send the recap on?

findings.text: Eight hosts, five themes and 38 quotes, each matched to its transcript line.
Six of eight check a recap line by hunting through the recording. Five of eight had seen a passing idea listed under Decisions.

Five of eight had a recap reach other people before they read it. In three cases the readers were outside the company: two customers and a job candidate. The synthesis says to treat that count with care, because the interviewer asked about it.

moment.label: The quote nobody said
moment.quote: If it showed me the exact moment, I would stop re-watching the call
moment.note: The request asked for this line. A script looked for it in all eight transcripts, did not find it, and removed it. Nothing was reworded to make it fit.

steps.changed: The counts became the evidence the plan was tested against. The pre-mortem's top risk rests on the five of eight whose recap went out before they had read it.

steps.question: If Auto-assign failed, why would it have failed?

findings.text: Ten failure stories across six areas. Three are marked as guesses, with no evidence either way.
The five worst each got a tripwire: a metric, a line it must not cross, a date and an owner. The first trips on one report of a wrong recap that reached an external guest in the pilot.
One risk hides the others. Nobody measures how often a recap line is wrong, so the tripwires could stay quiet while trust drops.

moment.label: The plan changed before the PRD was written

before.name: Auto-assign
before.text: Five minutes after a meeting, email the recap to every invitee, guests included, and turn every action item into a task. Nobody reviews it first.

after.name: Draft-first recap with sources
after.text: The host gets the draft first and chooses who gets it. Nothing is sent or assigned automatically.

steps.changed: The plan itself. Auto-assign never reached a PRD. The PRD that was written replaces it with a draft-first recap with sources.

steps.question: What exactly replaces Auto-assign, and in what order?

findings.text: Six numbered points in three sections: checking a line, who sees it and who owns it, and outsiders and doubt.
A rollout in three steps. The draft to the host and the split Decisions list go first, because neither needs another team. Two points wait on legal and a partner team.

No size is forecast. Four of the six points start from a baseline nobody has measured. The PRD also warns that one guardrail may favour auto-send, because a host who never reads the recap never reports it.

steps.changed: The test was set up as the PRD said: hosts split 50/50, draft-first against auto-send, with sharing a recap within 24 hours as the headline and two guardrails counted per host.

steps.question: What does each change actually look like?
Did the draft-first recap get more hosts to share?

findings.text: On the surface it was a clear win. Hosts who shared a recap within 24 hours rose 8.0 points, from 19.0% to 27.0%, and both guardrails fell.
The split was planned even. It came out as 31,204 hosts in control and 28,975 in draft first, and chance does not explain a gap that big.

The script checks the split before it reads the result, so rule 1 fired: sample ratio mismatch, do not trust the result. The likely cause was a remark made in passing. Control hosts were logged when the email was sent, and draft-first hosts when the draft screen loaded.

steps.changed: The decision. An 8.0 point gain was not shipped, and the next step is a fixed test, not a launch.

ending.body: On the surface this was the biggest win of the three cases. The readout says the gain may be real, partly real or not real, and that this test cannot say which. It asks for both groups to be logged at the same moment and for the test to be run again.
